<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with vivid, well-organized speeches, and both answered pressure questions in the required A1:/A2: format. PRO built a clean normative frame ("print the price," "guilt is not a payroll department") and landed two genuinely damaging rebuttals: the Meyer example as a unilateral-disarmament coordination failure, and the "one boss versus a boss plus table nine" reversal of CON's managerial-power point. It also forced a real concession from CON that the objection to a legally mandated pass-through was never opacity but amount. CON, however, won the decisive burden fight. The motion promises *higher base pay*, and CON repeatedly forced PRO onto the question of the number. PRO honestly conceded the top earner takes a cut and could only offer "whatever the owner can afford" for the median, then in closing said "honest prices are smaller than dishonest ones" — which CON converted into the sharpest voting line of the debate: the motion promises a raise and PRO's own defense is that pay shrinks, while the owner now sets 100% of it, the split, and the schedule. CON also neutralized PRO's arbitrage explanation with the full-minimum-plus-tips comparison and offered a live, less drastic alternative (raise the tipped minimum) that PRO answered only on honesty/harassment grounds, not on earnings. PRO's fairness and discrimination arguments remain partly live, and CON took execution costs for two clipped turns and for abandoning its own transparency pillar, but CON gave the cleaner reason to reject the proposition as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of PRO's "name the number" answer: after PRO conceded the high-earning server takes a cut and could only promise "whatever the owner can afford," CON crystallized it as "predictability of a pay cut is still a pay cut" and "the motion promises a raise and delivers the opposite," directly tying PRO's concession to the motion's own textual promise of higher base pay.</best_rebuttal>
